A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices A–D. Retained and revised content can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic system-identification experiments, real-world simulations, a 32-participant evaluation of 36 videos, and additional single-view and ablation results.

after.justification: V2 retains original simulation and human-evaluation results and adds quantitative motion evaluations and ablations in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same Gaussian reconstruction, GPT-4 material initialization, optical-flow guidance, and differentiable MLS-MPM optimization. PhysFlow is a newly explicit name; the PDFs do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same nine synthetic objects, nine real-world scenes, and single-view examples guided by PhysGen/Kling. The change from PhysGenBench to PhyGenBench retains the same cited source and examples. Large-force scenarios already appear in v1.

E2.justification: V2 newly includes PhysGaussian in the PhysGen-scene comparison (Table 8), whereas v1's corresponding single-view evaluation presents PhysGen/Kling-guided examples without this comparator. The main synthetic and real-world baseline sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Synthetic evaluation replaces AE/MAE with relative error and adds optical-flow EPE. Real-world and single-view evaluations add ECMS with alpha = 0.1. Physics3D's reported setting expands to elasticity with viscoelasticity. Section 4.2 also specifies GPT-derived materials for PhysGaussian, conflicting with Appendix B.2's manual initialization; these descriptions do not establish whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 substantially extends component validation with quantitative real-world ECMS ablations of initialization, optimization, and render versus flow guidance (Table 5; Figures 3 and 7). It also revises the synthetic loss-ablation evidence, including several qualitative outputs. V1's material-type and density ablation is retained.

E5.justification: The human-study sample size and rating-distribution reporting remain unchanged. Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests; the added evaluations do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds RE/EPE results and ECMS comparisons and ablations, including a real-world ECMS of 3.08 for the proposed method. Some ablation rankings change beyond normalization: flow beats render loss for Cat's Young's-modulus error in v1 Table 6, but v2 Table 10 reports render 0.167 versus flow 0.387 RE. Human-evaluation means remain unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 introduces the mathematical definition of ECMS in Equation 4, combining velocity-change, spatial-smoothness, and inverse-motion terms. The continuum-mechanics equations, optimization formulation, and material definitions are retained, with no new proofs or theorems.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about multimodal material initialization, optical-flow-guided parameter optimization, and realistic simulations across diverse materials. The PhysFlow name and two-innovation framing restate existing contributions.

C2.justification: V2 describes synthetic performance more specifically as competitive with GIC and interprets lower ECMS as more physically plausible motion. It also contextualizes baseline weaknesses under larger forces. The existing limitations concerning missing relighting, shadows, and specular effects remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds scene-specific force vectors, durations, and rotation/release settings in Table 7, and explicitly documents the render-loss formula. Its abstract states that code and data are available through the project page; v1 linked that page for videos. These are documentation changes, without external verification of availability.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to FlowNet, SeeGround, RayDF, and DDF-ISM. The broader positioning against existing reconstruction and physical-simulation methods remains stable; reference renumbering and bibliographic corrections do not constitute further substantive changes.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized introductory and experimental rewrites, explicitly names PhysFlow, updates appendix cross-references and a subsection title, and adds author-contact and acknowledgement text. The main section sequence and most methodological and explanatory prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation is substantially reorganized: separate synthetic comparison and loss-summary tables become a combined RE/EPE table with detailed appendix tables. V2 adds three ECMS tables, a force-duration table, and two annotated comparison figures, and revises synthetic ablation panels. Most other figures are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful quantitative motion comparisons, component ablations, and previously unspecified force settings. However, Table 9 obscures baseline attribution through loss-function headers that conflict with the matched baseline comparison and Table 10's identically labeled results. Section 4.2 and Appendix B.2 also disagree on PhysGaussian initialization. These new ambiguities affect central evaluation evidence, preventing a reliable assessment of whether the benefits outweigh the reporting problems.
